intel-foundry-hsbc-upgrade.headline: Intel's foundry turnaround becomes 'too good to ignore,' says HSBC
intel-foundry-hsbc-upgrade.body_md:
Frank Lee's team at HSBC did something Wall Street doesn't do lightly this week: they doubled a price target. Intel's, to be exact, from $100 to $200, while keeping the stock rated Buy. The bank now reckons there's another 60% of upside left in a stock that has already surged 233% since January — and the reason, for the first time, isn't really about chips going into laptops or servers. It's about the factory business Intel almost gave up on.

HSBC's note credits two things: Intel's server CPU shipments, which the bank now sees growing 25% year-over-year in 2026 (up from a 20% estimate), and — the newer piece — Intel Foundry, the contract manufacturing arm CEO Lip-Bu Tan has been trying to rebuild around the 18A process node. HSBC has started folding foundry into its sum-of-the-parts valuation for the first time, calling the business "too good to ignore now" as capacity bottlenecks ease and outside customers start kicking the tires.

![Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5b/Intel_CEO_Lip-Bu_Tan_%282025%29_%28cropped%29.jpg)

## The turnaround story, so far

Tan took over in March 2025 promising discipline after Pat Gelsinger's ouster — cutting 15,000 jobs, killing side projects, chasing roughly $10 billion in annual savings. The bet paid off on the stock chart: Intel shares have run from around $22 to well over $100 in the past year, a 462% gain that has made the company one of the most talked-about turnaround trades in the market. Panther Lake, the first laptop chip built on the 18A node, is now shipping, and Intel says yields have been climbing 7-8% a month. Nvidia and SoftBank have both taken stakes. Reports have floated engagements with Tesla, Apple, SpaceX and Google.

What hasn't happened yet is the one thing that would settle the argument: a committed anchor customer for Intel's next node, 14A. Management has said publicly it won't build 14A capacity without firm external orders in hand — a scar from years of overbuilding capacity nobody used — and as of Intel's most recent earnings call, it had none. The company is pointing to the second half of 2026 as the window when test-chip customers are expected to decide. HSBC's upgrade is, in effect, a bet that they will.

## A market already ahead of the story

The timing is the awkward part. HSBC published its note on a day Intel shares fell about 6% to $119.83, part of a broader semiconductor pullback — AMD dropped 5%, the SOXX chip ETF fell 6% — that traders characterized as profit-taking rather than anything company-specific. Cantor Fitzgerald also raised its Intel target that week, to $150 from $90, so HSBC wasn't alone in reaching for a bigger number even as the stock gave some back.

That's the tension in the HSBC call: it isn't wrong that foundry has stopped being a pure liability, but a 233% year-to-date rally means most of that improvement is arguably already in the price. Intel Foundry still posted roughly $2.4 billion in operating losses in the first quarter. The bull case rests on customer commitments that, by Intel's own account, don't exist yet. HSBC is pricing in the second half of 2026 playing out as hoped; nothing in the note describes what happens to the stock if it doesn't.

## What comes next

The test is concrete and dated: Intel has pointed to the back half of 2026 for the first firm 14A customer decisions, and that announcement — or its absence — will matter more to the foundry narrative than any single analyst note. Until then, HSBC's $200 target reads less like new information about Intel's factories than a reminder of how far sentiment has already run ahead of them.

european-stocks-surge.headline: European stocks rally, oil slips as defense and luxury shares lead
european-stocks-surge.body_md:
European equities closed higher Thursday in a session with an odd pairing at the top of the leaderboard: arms makers and handbag makers. The Euro Stoxx 50 added 1.37% to close near 6,370, with defense contractors and luxury-goods houses supplying most of the lift, while crude oil kept sliding — Brent fell below $71 a barrel, its lowest level since late February.

Rheinmetall led the defense bloc, up 6.07%, with Thales adding 2.05%, Saab 3.32% and BAE Systems 1.95%. The push came a day after London published its Defence Investment Plan — an extra £15 billion ($20 billion) layered onto existing budgets, part of a £298 billion package over four years that lifts UK defense spending to £79.1 billion, or 2.7% of GDP, by 2029. Roughly £5 billion of that is earmarked for drones and autonomous systems, £8.2 billion for the UK-Italy-Japan Tempest stealth-fighter programme, and £64 billion for renewing the nuclear deterrent, including new Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS submarines.

![The Louis Vuitton flagship store on Paris's Avenue des Champs-Élysées](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3a/Louis_Vuitton_flagship_store_at_Avenue_des_Champs-%C3%89lys%C3%A9es_%2822288053650%29.jpg)

LVMH, meanwhile, gained 1.6%, extending a firmer run across the luxury names that had been among the hardest hit by the Middle East conflict that broke out in February. The Gulf has been a fast-growing market for the sector even through a broader, years-long slump tied to soft Chinese demand, which is why luxury stocks have moved almost in lockstep with war-risk headlines since. Thursday's driver was oil: shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has climbed above 10 million barrels a day with US naval support, Iranian exports have topped 40 million barrels since Washington lifted its blockade, and record Russian seaborne volumes have added to a general glut. All of that, plus signs of progress in indirect US-Iran talks, pushed Brent to its lowest since before the war started and WTI toward $68.

## Same rally, two different engines

The pairing looks contradictory only at first glance. Luxury is rising because investors read the oil slide as confirmation that Gulf demand and shipping risk are normalizing — a straightforward de-escalation trade. Defense is rising for close to the opposite reason: European governments are locking in higher structural spending regardless of how the Iran conflict resolves, a commitment now large enough — Germany's Rheinmetall-led buildout, the UK's £298 billion plan — to keep order books full for years. The two sectors are pricing different variables, which is exactly why they can rally on the same day.

The near-term test is whether the peace track holds. Doha talks were already delicate, and they now face a delay after the death of Iran's former Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei, whose funeral begins July 4. Any relapse would send oil — and luxury shares — back the other way; the defense trade, tied to multi-year budget lines rather than headlines, would be far less exposed.

benzinga-top-tickers-june.headline: SpaceX and Marvell crash the most-searched list, Micron stays on top
benzinga-top-tickers-june.body_md:
Every month, Benzinga Pro tallies which stock tickers its subscribers type into the search bar most often — a rough proxy for what retail and professional traders alike are paying attention to. The June list, out this week, has a familiar name at the top and two new arrivals that tell their own story about the month that was.

Micron Technology held the number-one spot for a second straight month, no great surprise for a stock that closed at an all-time high of $1,213.56 on June 25 after reporting fiscal third-quarter revenue up 346% to $41.5 billion and gross margins near 85%. Micron shares are up roughly 300% for the year — the kind of chart that keeps a ticker pinned to the top of anyone's search history.

The more interesting story is who joined the list. SpaceX debuted on the Nasdaq on June 12 under the ticker SPCX, in what became the largest IPO in history — a $75 billion raise on a $1.77 trillion valuation, with Elon Musk retaining more than 82% of the voting power. Shares priced at $135, opened at $150, and closed their first day up about 19%. Benzinga's data team called SpaceX's entry at number three "one of the highest ever initial entries" on its leaderboard — a striking result given the stock had been public for less than two-thirds of the month it was being measured.

![SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launch](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b2/SpaceX_Falcon_9_rocket_launches_NASA%27s_TRACERS_mission_from_Vandenberg%2C_California.jpg)

## A search list is not a scoreboard

Marvell Technology rounded out the notable new entries at number five, having tripled in value this year on the strength of AI-chip demand. The stock jumped more than 25% in a single session in early June after Nvidia's Jensen Huang, speaking at Computex Taipei, called Marvell a "trillion-dollar candidate" — Nvidia had put roughly $2 billion behind the company. The rally kept going: UBS raised its price target to $340 from $230 on June 30, citing Marvell's position in CXL data-center interconnect technology.

The rest of the top 12 — SPY, Tesla, Nvidia, Intel, SanDisk, Apple, a small-cap called Freecast, Oracle and Broadcom — reads like a snapshot of where trader attention concentrated during a chip-heavy month. Nebius, IREN, Qualcomm and Rocket Lab all fell out of the rankings from May.

What the list doesn't do is tell anyone whether searching a ticker preceded buying it, selling it, or just gawking at the chart. Benzinga doesn't publish a search-to-trade correlation, so the ranking works better as a mood board for retail attention than as a signal to act on. SpaceX's first full month of public trading, and whether its search volume converts into sustained volume on the tape, will be a better test of that question than its debut-month novelty.

floor.body_md:

BSX and PEP hit intraday take-profit after sharp bounces, accounting for 58% of total P&L—the capitulation thesis correct and fast. No news, no overnight holds required, just mechanical demand snapback into an oversold read.

The lighter side of the book stayed quiet. GLEN.L flatlined despite the tighter stop for executive uncertainty, and BP.L exited on schedule without reversing either. Two small losses erased only 3% of the gains, but flagged the real constraint: the oversold bounce works when volume backs it. Tomorrow's question is whether yesterday's setup continues to offer fresh entry points or whether the reversal window is already closing.
